Abstract
The rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sig-
nificantly increased hardware demands. Wafer-scale chips, which
integrate numerous compute units on an entire wafer, offer a high-
density computing solution for data centers and can extend Moore’s
Law at system level. However, current wafer-scale data center ar-
chitectures face inefficiencies, such as uncoordinated resource al-
location and lack of co-optimization for system area, preventing
optimal integration density and performance within given cost
and physical constraints. We propose a co-exploration approach of
computing and hardware architectures to bridge this gap.
We first develop an optimized wafer-scale single-cabinet data
center model, integrating configurable on-chip memory dies and
employing a vertically stacked hardware architecture. Based on this
model, we introduce Titan, an automated exploration framework
for intra-chip and inter-chip architecture design and optimization.
Based on the architecture features of wafer-scale systems with opti-
mal integration density, Titan establishes parameter dependencies
to co-design the computing and hardware architectures. To reduce
the design cycle for wafer-scale systems, Titan introduces vertical
area constraints and pre-checks physical limits by integrating a
series of reliability prediction models. It also integrates hardware

Introduction
In recent years, the rapid development of large language models
(LLMs) has driven a surge in parameter scales and increasingly
complex model architectures, placing higher demands on hard-
ware platforms in terms of computational performance, bandwidth,
memory capacity, and scalability [4, 31].
Constrained by physical limits, transistor density within a sin-
gle chip has approached its practical ceiling, making it hard for
Moore’s Law [33] to extend at the chip size level. The exponential

demand for computing performance from LLM training has pro-

However, in conventional GPU clusters, non-computational devices
(e.g., switches, I/O devices) [24, 43] occupy a significant portion
of system resources, and this kind of waste gets even larger as
computing scale increases. As shown in Fig. 1-a, there is a sharp de-
cline in the system’s overall transistor density from single chips to
multi-GPU distributed clusters and further to data centers, creating
a substantial gap between achieved density and physical limit.
In contrast, Wafer-scale chips offer a highly integrated com-
puting solution [6, 11–13, 26, 55] for LLM training. Wafer-scale
chips densely integrate massive compute cores and make short-
reach interconnects on a single wafer (up to 40,000 mm2 in area
[29, 45]), while they integrate non-computational modules (e.g.,
power supply modules, external connectors, and cooling modules)
in the vertical space [9] to make full use of 3D spatial resources.
This architecture can effectively fill the density gap inherent in
GPU clusters, extending Moore’s Law systemically and delivering
substantial performance gains [37].
For instance, a Cerebras CS-3 cabinet integrates a wafer-scale
chip (WSE-3) with 2.6 trillion transistors and 850,000 cores [22, 27,
30], capable of delivering up to 26 exaFLOPS of FP16 performance–
comparable to or exceeding the capabilities of tens of thousands
of GPUs for certain AI models [3]. Similarly, each Dojo ExaPOD
[5] incorporates 120 training tiles with 3,000 D1 chips and over 100
trillion transistors, achieving 1.1 exaFLOPS of FP16 performance.
Besides available on-chip abundant computing resources and
high-speed bandwidth in wafer-scale chips, the system can support
the exclusive use of data parallelism when training LLMs. This elim-
inates the painful steps necessary in distributed computing using
GPU clusters, delivering near-perfect linear scaling across hundreds
of millions of AI-optimized compute cores [45] (see Fig. 1-b). To con-
sider the cost-effectiveness (see Fig. 1), larger chips inherently entail
higher manufacturing costs, yet they yield substantial performance
improvements. With advancements in process technology, the feasi-
ble threshold for chip sizes offering higher cost-effectiveness contin-
ues to expand. Concurrently, reduced requirements for interconnect
components, thermal management modules, and other ancillary
systems within the system architecture ensure that systems con-
structed with larger chips exhibit superior performance per unit
cost within a specific scale threshold [2].
To maximize system performance under fixed cost constraints,
the design of wafer-scale system architecture presents substantial
unexplored optimization potential. There are still inefficiencies in
current mature wafer-scale chip architecture, revealing two criti-
cal optimization instructions when designing both the computing
and hardware architecture. (1) Continuously increasing intra-chip
compute resources does not always lead to stable performance im-
provements, necessitating a balance between computational and
memory resources within the chip. (2) Maximizing the area of a
single chip does not necessarily ensure the highest integration den-
sity or cost efficiency for the data center, emphasizing the need for
coordinated optimization across multiple physical layers.
Thus, we argue that co-designing the computing and hard-
ware architectures of wafer-scale chips is essential to achieve
the optimal integration density and performance for wafer-scale
data centers in a given space and cost. This requires the coordi-
nated allocation of resources within the computing architecture
for better performance utilization, alongside system-level area co-
optimization for cross-layer modules for better integration density.
However, achieving the co-design of computing and hardware
architectures in wafer-scale data centers presents the following
challenges: (1) Lack of fine-grained modeling: The absence of a
fine-grained parameterized model for wafer-scale chips and cabi-
nets makes it difficult to achieve coordinated optimization under
a unified framework [36]; (2) Extensive design space: Wafer-scale
cabinet design encompasses a vast design space, and traditional
optimization algorithms of design space exploration (DSE) are inef-
fective due to overlooking the unique characteristics of wafer-scale
architectures; (3) Lack of comprehensive validation and evaluation
frameworks: Wafer-scale chip architectures face packaging reliabil-
ity challenges, yet insufficient design-phase validation in current
tools necessitates multiple iterations and prolonged cycles. Addi-
tionally, the inability to effectively balance performance and cost
arises from the lack of comprehensive evaluation systems.
Toward the optimal integration density and performance in a
given system cost and physical constraints, we first construct an
optimized architecture model for the wafer-scale single-cabinet data
center, encompassing both computing and hardware architectures.
This model emphasizes coordinated allocation of computational
and memory resources, integrating configurable memory dies and
computing dies within the same wafer-scale package.
Simultaneously, we address system-level area optimization by
a vertically stacked infrastructure of the wafer-scale chip system
with a cross-layer vertical area constraint. This optimization can
greatly improve design efficiency while ensuring the validation and
optimality of the design results.
Building on these two architecture optimizations, we propose
Titan, an automated exploration framework for intra-chip and
inter-chip architecture design and optimization. Titan enables
the collaborative design of computing and hardware architectures
to optimize system performance and supports physical constraint
pre-checks under varying hardware requirements. Titan is able to
design the optimal architecture configuration efficiently within a
huge wafer-scale cabinet design space.

In summary, our contributions include:
1) We demonstrate the feasibility and advantages of wafer-scale
chips for data center constructions and highlight existing inef-
ficiencies in computing and hardware architectures to propose
necessity of wafer-scale architecture design synergistically.
2) We develop a parameterized wafer-scale single-cabinet archi-
tecture model with vertical area constraints and configurable
on-wafer memory dies, which achieves coordinated resource
allocation and system area co-optimization.
3) We propose Titan, an automated exploration framework com-
prising Intra-Chip Architecture Designer, Inter-Chip Cabinet
Designer, and System Evaluator, to efficiently co-design the com-
puting and hardware architectures of wafer-scale systems.
4) We validate the practicality and superiority of Titan through
experiments on various application scenarios, showing an aver-
age improvement by 2.90× computing performance, 2.11× com-
munication bandwidth, and 11.23× off-die memory bandwidth
compared to a Dojo-like tray architecture under the same cost
constraint. Moreover, we leverage Titan to uncover insights into
the optimal single-chip area choice within a cabinet under differ-
ent cost constraints.

Background and Motivation
2.1
Opportunities in Wafer-scale Datacenters
Recent advancements in LLMs, such as GPT and PaLM, have intro-
duced unprecedented challenges to hardware in terms of comput-
ing performance, memory, and bandwidth to support fast training.
Emerging wafer-scale chips provide a compact and efficient alter-
native for data center computing by integrating numerous compute
units on a single wafer, delivering GPU cluster-level performance
within a monolithic wafer-scale chip.
In addition, wafer-scale chips feature short-reach interconnects
and high-density connectivity, effectively addressing bandwidth
bottlenecks and energy inefficiencies associated with traditional
board-level and inter-cabinet interconnects under the same com-
puting requirements. This design greatly improves bandwidth and
compute density, making it an ideal choice for LLM training.
To achieve high integration density, wafer-scale systems adopt
a specialized vertical integration architecture and infrastructure
with custom-designed modules. Taking Tesla Dojo as an example
(see Fig. 2-a) [5][46], a Dojo Training Tile consists of a 5×5 D1 chip
array, closely packed within an interposer package with power and
thermal module using TSMC’s InFO_SoW packaging technology
[9]. On-chip communication is facilitated through metal routing
within the interposer, eliminating traditional PCB-based intercon-
nects. A liquid cooling module is tightly coupled to the chip surface,
utilizing direct liquid cooling to efficiently dissipate heat. The back-
side of the interposer is directly connected to Voltage Regulation
Modules (VRM) and high-speed I/O interfaces for stable power
delivery and external data communication. This forms a vertically
stacked system that can independently perform AI model training
tasks. Multiple such systems are interconnected through Dojo’s
proprietary high-speed switch network, enabling further expansion
into a wafer-scale cabinet that delivers data center-level compute
performance.
Compared with traditional GPU cluster architectures, wafer-
scale system architectures natively feature numerous advantages
and substantial potential (see Fig. 2-b). In this vertically stacked ar-
chitecture, inter-chip communication is facilitated by high-density
interconnects embedded within the InFO redistribution layers (RDL),
eliminating external PCB traces and discrete switch modules found
in conventional GPU clusters. This design achieves a higher system-
level compute density (1.1 EFLOPS /mm2 for a Dojo training tile
vs. 0.2 EFLOPS/mm2 for H100 GPU clusters). The InFO_SoW pack-
aging enables a 5 𝜇m microbump pitch and 3D routing density
of 500 traces/mm2, effectively reducing inter-chip signal transmis-
sion distance to <5 mm (compared to 50-100 mm PCB traces in
multi-chip GPU architectures). This results in a higher tile-level
bandwidth than NVIDIA’s NVLink interconnect system (242TB/s
IO bandwidth within a Cerebras WSE3 vs. 7.2TB/s IO bandwidth of
a GPU cluster with 8×𝐻100 [29]). Additionally, unlike GPU clusters,
wafer-scale systems remove the need for external NVLink switches,
optical interconnects, and additional power/cooling infrastructure.
For equivalent exascale performance, the Wafer-scale chip system
can greatly reduce component counts and reduce system power
consumption, substantially lowering cost per TFLOP (Tesla Dojo
will have 4.0× better performance and 1.3× better performance/watt
with a larger chip size [34]).
2.2
Limitations of Current Wafer-scale System
Designs
Despite the significant advantages of wafer-scale chips, there are
still inefficiencies in computing and hardware architectures of cur-
rent mature wafer-scale products. As a result, expanded data centers
fail to achieve optimal integration density and performance. We
analyze the specific limitations and propose corresponding improve-
ments.

2.2.1
Inefficiencies in computing architecture fail to coordinate com-
pute and memory resource. Dojo and Cerebras WSE employ Wafer-
Scale Integration (WSI) architectures, integrating numerous com-
pute cores and high-capacity SRAM on a single chip. This design
significantly enhances performance for small-scale model training
since the total parameters can be stored on the wafer, fully leverag-
ing the on-wafer computing performance and bandwidth. However,
these architectures face limitations when scaling to large models.
The on-chip memory capacity and off-wafer bandwidth constraints
hinder the accommodation of extensive model parameters, lead-
ing to performance bottlenecks due to frequent off-wafer memory
accesses with lower bandwidth and higher latency.
To address these challenges, integrating memory dies directly
onto the wafer alongside compute dies presents a viable solution.
This "on-wafer memory" architecture enables tight coupling of
computation and memory capacity, optimizing memory hierarchy
and bandwidth utilization. Fig. 3 illustrates the comparison of differ-
ent performance metrics between off-wafer memory and on-wafer
memory architectures. In contrast to traditional off-wafer memory
architectures, on-wafer memory can balance compute, memory
capacity, on-die bandwidth, and off-die bandwidth, thereby enhanc-
ing performance and scalability for large models. This on-wafer
memory architecture is widely used in chiplet-based systems such
as NVIDIA H100 [8] and H200 GPU, leveraging TSMC’s CoWoS-S
package technology [13]. As TSMC continues to improve its pack-
age technology aimed at larger package sizes [39], this architecture
is promising in wafer-scale chip design.
2.2.2
Inefficiencies in hardware architecture fail to reach system-
level integration density limits. Although Cerebras WSE-3 achieves
high-density integration at the chip level with 900,000 AI cores
and 4 trillion transistors [28], its cabinet design suffers from lim-
ited integration density. These constraints stem from differences in
hardware architecture. WSE-3’s frustration (such as power deliv-
ery modules, external connectors, and cooling) are not vertically
stacked but are instead deployed independently (see Fig. 4-a), re-
sulting in lower integration density within the cabinet. A single
CS-3 cabinet can accommodate only one WSE-3 chip and cannot
be further expanded, limiting its scalability. For larger LLMs and
deeper training, the inability to add more chips within the cabinet
to enhance overall system performance becomes a bottleneck.

In contrast, Dojo adopts a vertically stacked architecture (see
Fig. 2 and Fig. 4-b). Six Dojo tiles form a tray, and multiple trays
can be integrated into a cabinet. This vertical-stacked approach
significantly enhances the compute density, enabling high-density
integration of multiple wafer-scale chips within the same cabinet
while maintaining excellent scalability. Inspired by Dojo’s vertical
hardware architecture, we adopt the similar vertical architecture
for the hardware design of wafer-scale chips and cabinets.
However, in Dojo’s vertical architecture, the compute layer oc-
cupies significantly less physical area than other supporting layers
(see the top of Fig. 4-b). To improve integration density, it is possible
to coordinate the design of all layers within the vertical system,
ensuring their areas align closely with the compute layer (see the
bottom of Fig. 4-b). This approach optimizes vertical space utiliza-
tion, enabling higher system integration density.
2.3
Challenges in Wafer-scale Cabinet Design
The co-design of computing and hardware architecture is essen-
tial to achieve optimal integration density and performance in
wafer-scale cabinets. This requires simultaneous consideration of
coordinated resource allocation within the computing architecture
and the co-optimization of system area. To address these needs, an
automated co-design and optimization framework is necessary. We
identify three key challenges of wafer-scale cabinet design:
(1) Lack of fine-grained parameterized architectural ab-
stractions and dependency modeling. Current wafer-scale cab-
inet designs lack fine-grained abstraction models from compute
cores to chips and cabinets. There is no unified modeling of com-
puting and hardware architectures, nor quantified dependencies
across design layers. This makes it difficult to build a parameterized
co-design framework, hindering the balance and optimization of
compute, storage, and bandwidth demands within the cabinet.
(2) Huge design space and optimization complexity. De-
signing a wafer-scale cabinet encompasses various aspects, such as

comprehensive evaluation systems, making it difficult to reliably
balance performance and cost during the design process.
To address these challenges, we first construct models of an
optimal wafer-scale chip and cabinet architecture, and parameterize
their design space (Section 3). Based on the characteristics of wafer-
scale systems, we propose a design space exploration path tailored
for wafer-scale cabinet architectures (see Fig. 5).
This path begins with the intra-chip architecture design, extract-
ing a set of independent design parameters from the intra-chip
search space, with each parameter set corresponding to a com-
plete chip architecture configuration. By establishing a mapping
relationship through the chip’s internal dependency models, we
significantly reduce the original exploration space. Subsequently,
the validity of each configuration is checked (including interposer
reliability, system area, power, etc.), and the performance and cost
are evaluated. Next, we design the cabinet, selecting a subset from
the valid chip design space and combining it with the cabinet-
level search space to obtain a set of independent cabinet design
parameters. After sequentially performing constraint checks and
evaluations, all cabinet configurations that meet the design require-
ments and constraints form a space, from which the optimal cabinet
design is selected based on the optimization objective.
To realize this design flow, we design an automated exploration
framework Titan (Section 4).
3
Hierarchical Cabinet Architecture Model
This chapter introduces a fine-grained parameterized wafer-scale
cabinet architectural model in computing and hardware aspects,
followed by a hierarchical definition of its parameter space based
on intra-chip and inter-chip levels.
Figure 6: Computing and hardware architecture models of
wafer-scale cabinets in intra-chip and inter-chip levels.
3.1
Computing Architecture
Fig. 6-a shows a hierarchical diagram of the computing architecture
of the entire wafer-scale cabinet model, which flows from cores
to know-good-dies (KGDs) to chips to a cabinet. The inter-chip
computing architecture contains a mesh-routed chip array and
several sets of host interface boards (HIBs), which provide external
DRAM storage and interface to communicate with hosts within a
cabinet. A set of HIBs is interconnected to a peripheral chip through
outer connectors. The number of HIB set is determined by the input
memory capacity demand.
The intra-chip computing architecture contains a configurable
KGD array interconnected by a mesh network, and multiple mem-
ory dies and IO dies distributed around the periphery of the KGD
array. Memory dies and IO dies are equipped for sufficient intra-chip
memory and inter-chip communication, respectively. The number
of memory dies is configurable (including 0), making the model
adaptable to conventional wafer-scale architecture. Each KGD in-
cludes a configurable computing core array by a mesh network-
on-chip (NoC), and a set of die-to-die (D2D) interface (i.e., PHYs)
around it, which is used to data transfer between adjacent KGDs
or KGDs to memory dies and IO dies. Each core is models as a
combination of multiply-accumulate (MAC) units, SRAM and NoC
routers.
3.2
Hardware Architecture
Fig. 6-b illustrates the hardware architecture of the wafer-scale chip
and cabinet model, which adopts a vertically stacked infrastructure.
Within a single cabinet, an extendable chip array, an HIB array,
host, and power supply are vertically stacked. The HIB is a relatively
independent system equipped with its own control unit. In this
design, we employ standard Dojo interconnect boards [5], each
featuring 2×16GB HBM, a 50GB/s Ethernet interface, and a 32GB/s
Gen4 PCIe interface. These boards provide 900GB/s bandwidth for
inter-chip communication via two connectors.

The intra-chip hardware architecture is divided into four func-
tional physical layers, arranged from top to bottom: the cooling
layer, computing layer, interconnect layer, and substrate layer.
The cooling layer is bonded on the chip’s surface with various
values of thermal efficiency. The computing layer is modeled as the
intra-chip computing architecture with all I/Os fanning out from
the bottom. Assuming the use of TSMC’s InFO_SoW packaging
technology [9], the interconnect layer is a large interposer with
multiple metal interconnect layers, which include routing layers
and power distribution network (PDN). Its top and bottom surfaces
are bonded with microbumps [23] and C4bumps [35], respectively,
and it also contains a large number of Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).
The substrate layer, which is bonded at the interposer backside,
is modeled as a multi-layer PCB structure, integrating VRMs and
external connectors.
Our intra-chip hardware architecture comprehensively considers
the hardware configuration of a standalone wafer-scale system,
which serves as the minimal scalable unit in wafer-scale cabinet
design. By defining independent functional modules, the model
allows for flexible adaptation to different technologies.
3.3
Parameter Space
The wafer-scale cabinet architecture model demonstrates excep-
tional flexibility, with its computing and hardware architectures
jointly offering a range of designable parameters. Table 1 lists the
design parameters categorized into two levels: intra-chip and inter-
chip, forming the design space for the collaborative design frame-
work, Titan.
Given the vast design space, traditional search or heuristic algo-
rithms fail to explore it comprehensively within a limited timeframe,
and the discrete nature of parameter ranges risks overlooking op-
timal solutions. For intra-chip design, we establish a search space
using mutually independent parameters within the computing and
interconnect layers (marked in Table 1). By modeling the depen-
dency, each set of design parameters in this space can correspond to
a complete architecture configuration, which significantly reduces
the search space.

4.1
Titan Overview
Based on the parameterized architecture model, we further propose
Titan, a framework designed for the architecture co-design and
optimization of wafer-scale cabinets. Titan enables the collaborative
design of computing and hardware architectures and pre-checks
physical constraints under varying hardware requirements.
Titan establishes dependency relationships among intra-chip and
inter-chip design parameters, so that parts of the design parameters
can be mapped to a complete architecture design. This significantly
reduces the search space and enhances design efficiency. Addition-
ally, Titan checks system and package constraints by developing a
series of reliability prediction models, which can eliminate a large
number of invalid architecture configurations in the early design
stage. Titan also evaluates both performance and cost, allowing for
trade-offs among multiple metrics during optimization.

4.2.3
Intra-layer Architecture Design and Constraints. Wafer-scale
chip architectures exhibit strong system-level dependencies. Ne-
glecting physical constraints during design can lead to violations in
the physical verification phase, necessitating costly redesign itera-
tions. Given the significant time overhead of full-chip verification at
wafer scale, repeated iterations severely degrade design efficiency.
Therefore, it is critical to proactively integrate physical constraints
in early design stages and establish rapid approximate models for
preliminary evaluation.
Drawing on relevant studies [18], [15], [49], [52], [7], [17], [54],

For medium-scale model training, such as BERT or GPT-2, the
performance bottleneck primarily arises from on-chip off-die mem-

optimization target parameters corresponding to (1,1,1). For larger-

parameters corresponding to (1,10,10).
Our experiments utilize the Astra-sim2.0 simulator [51] with
simplified assumptions (ignoring congestion and routing control).
Referred from Google’s Mesh Ring [21] communication algorithm,

5.4
Design Considerations for Single-chip Area
Under different cost constraints, Fig. 14 illustrates the relation-
ship between the area of intra-chip systems and performance per
unit cost of cabinets constructed from these chips, assuming the
optimization objective (1,1,1). Each point represents a feasible con-
figuration. For a specific total cost constraint, the largest chip area
does not always yield the optimal cabinet configuration. Under
tighter cost constraints, smaller chips are typically chosen due to
cost limitations. As the cost constraint relaxes, larger chips, offer-
ing higher on-chip resources and integration density, are favored.
However, factors such as total numbers of chips and the chip cost
must also be considered.
Due to the discrete nature of chip array configurations, the rela-
tionship between the chip area and cabinet cost-efficiency exhibits
a piecewise oscillatory trend: within certain ranges, cabinet perfor-
mance first increases and then decreases as the chip area grows.
Based on this, we propose a design insight: Increasing the area
of a single chip under the maximum wafer area constraint
benefits the construction of large-scale data centers. How-
ever, under fixed cost constraints, this does not always result
in optimal cost-efficiency performance. Discrete array con-
figurations and single-chip costs must also be taken into
account.
6
Conclusion
In this work, we design an optimized wafer-scale cabinet architec-
ture for a datacenter. The computing architecture integrates con-
figurable on-wafer memory dies, while the hardware architecture
adopts a vertically stacked structure for functional layers within a
single chip. It expand with a horizontally scalable cluster config-
uration for the inter-chip level. This design enables coordinated
resource allocation and area co-optimization, enhancing resource
utilization and integration density. Based on this architecture, we
developed a architecture model and proposed Titan, a framework
aimed at the co-design and optimization of wafer-scale cabinet
architectures. Titan considers the trade-offs between performance
and cost, exploring co-design strategies to maximize integration
density under cost and physical constraints, ultimately achieving
optimal performance.

Abstract: The rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sig- nificantly increased hardware demands. Wafer-scale chips, which integrate numerous compute units on an entire wafer, offer a high- density computing solution for data centers and can extend Moore’s Law at system level. However, current wafer-scale data center ar- chitectures face inefficiencies, such as uncoordinated resource al- location and lack of co-optimization for system area, preventing optimal integration density and performance within given cost and physical constraints. We propose a co-exploration approach of computing and hardware architectures to bridge this gap. We first develop an optimized wafer-scale single-cabinet data center model, integrating configurable on-chip memory dies and employing a vertically stacked hardware architecture. Based on this model, we introduce Titan, an automated exploration framework for intra-chip and inter-chip architecture design and optimization. Based on the architecture features of wafer-scale systems with opti- mal integration density, Titan establishes parameter dependencies to co-design the computing and hardware architectures. To reduce the design cycle for wafer-scale systems, Titan introduces vertical area constraints and pre-checks physical limits by integrating a series of reliability prediction models. Under the same cost constraint, on average, Titan’s cabinet design architecture improves system computing capacity by 2.90×, communication bandwidth by 2.11×, and memory bandwidth by 11.23× compared to the state-of-the-art Dojo-like wafer-scale single tray architecture. Simulated in different scenarios, Titan’s design delivers 3.17× and 10.66× performance improvement for Llama2-7B and Llama2-72B. Moreover, we leverage Titan to uncover insights into the optimal single-chip area choice within a cabinet under different cost constraints.
